pharm: An opium-derived alkaloid that suppresses the cough reflex centrally without significant analgesic, sedative, or dependence-producing opioid activity; also has weak sigma-receptor and antitussive actions.
quick: Typically 25-50 mg three to four times daily for dry cough (per EMA/national labels)
May be taken with or without food
Avoid unless clearly needed; limited data and some genotoxicity concern
No specific adjustment established; use cautiously
Cough response; bleeding/INR if on warfarin
summary: Noscapine is a naturally occurring benzylisoquinoline alkaloid from opium that is used as a centrally acting cough suppressant. Unlike codeine and other opioids, it has negligible analgesic effect and little or no potential for dependence or respiratory depression at usual doses. It is used widely outside the United States (e.g., under EMA and various national/BNF-style labels) for the symptomatic relief of dry, non-productive cough. It is not an FDA-approved drug in the United States. A notable interaction is potentiation of warfarin, increasing INR and bleeding risk.
indications: Symptomatic relief of dry, irritating, non-productive cough

dosage.d: Approximately 25-50 mg three to four times daily (per EMA/national product labels)
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest time

dosage.d: Weight/age-adjusted per national label; many products restrict use in young children
dosage.n: Follow local pediatric labeling; avoid in very young children

admin: Take with or without food for short-term symptomatic relief of dry cough
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period needed
Reassess if cough persists beyond about 1 week, worsens, or is accompanied by fever, rash, or persistent headache
Follow national/EMA product labeling for pediatric age and dose restrictions
Monitor INR closely if the patient is taking warfarin
moa: Noscapine suppresses the cough reflex through a central action on the medullary cough center, distinct from the opioid analgesic alkaloids of opium. Although structurally related to opium alkaloids, it lacks meaningful mu-opioid agonist activity and therefore does not produce analgesia, euphoria, or significant respiratory depression at antitussive doses. It exhibits weak sigma-receptor binding and bronchodilator/antispasmodic properties, and (at high experimental concentrations) interferes with microtubule dynamics, but the clinically relevant effect is central cough suppression.

absolute: Productive cough where suppression is undesirable (relative/absolute per label)

preg: Data are limited and some studies raise genotoxicity concerns; several authorities advise avoiding noscapine in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, unless clearly necessary. Use only if the benefit outweighs the potential risk and no safer alternative is available.
lact: There are limited data on noscapine excretion in human milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding and prefer non-pharmacologic measures or better-characterized alternatives where possible.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment has been established. Use with caution in significant renal impairment and follow national labeling.
hepatic: Noscapine is metabolized in the liver; use with caution in hepatic impairment as clearance may be reduced.

major: Warfarin - noscapine can markedly increase the anticoagulant effect and INR, raising bleeding risk; avoid or monitor INR closely
moderate: CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitors/substrates - noscapine is metabolized by these enzymes; interactions possible
CNS depressants - possible additive sedation in susceptible individuals
minor: Other antitussives - avoid combining cough suppressants
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no major food interaction established.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; possible additive central effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong INR/prothrombin time when combined with warfarin.

serious: Increased bleeding when combined with warfarin

monitoring: Persistence of cough beyond ~1 week (reassess for underlying cause)
counsel: Use this only for a short time to relieve a dry, tickly cough
See your doctor if the cough lasts more than about a week, brings up phlegm or blood, or comes with fever or chest pain
Tell your doctor if you take warfarin, as this medicine can increase its blood-thinning effect
It may cause mild drowsiness; be cautious if driving until you know how it affects you
Stop and seek help if you get a rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing
pk: Cough suppression about 4-6 hours per dose
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the United States; used under EMA/national/BNF labeling - dosing reflects those sources, not an FDA label
Non-opioid antitussive with negligible analgesia and very low dependence/respiratory-depression risk
Clinically important interaction: potentiates warfarin and raises INR - monitor or avoid
Best for dry, non-productive cough; not appropriate for productive cough where clearance is needed
Some genotoxicity signals make avoidance in pregnancy prudent
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not take a double dose. As an as-needed cough medicine, simply take the next dose when the cough returns.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, nausea, and in large amounts CNS effects; serious toxicity is uncommon. Manage supportively with monitoring; there is no specific antidote. Contact a poison control center for significant ingestion.
